finding: Government supplied 40%-61% of Calvary's revenue in every year FY15-FY25 on the audit basis (line 1e for FY24-25), and most of the growth since FY19.
evidence_summary: Audit-basis share 37% FY14 -> 50% FY21 -> 61% FY22 -> 51% FY23; line 1e 45% FY24, 58% FY25. Revenue $2.49M FY19 -> $4.97M FY25.
implication_for_calvary: Calvary is a government-anchored organization; private growth has not kept pace.

finding: FY25 ran a $607K deficit with contributions down $0.8M and the cash cushion at 4.4 months, versus 7.5 months in FY21.
evidence_summary: Revenue $4.97M vs expenses $5.58M; contributions $5.55M -> $4.75M; months of cash 7.5 -> 4.4.
implication_for_calvary: Little room to absorb a government cut; a reserve floor and a private-revenue recovery plan are both needed.

finding: Event contributions fell from $538K (FY24) to $55K (FY25), the largest single private-revenue swing.
evidence_summary: 990 Part VIII line 1c: $457,758 FY23, $538,070 FY24, $54,730 FY25; net special-event income negative every year through FY24.
implication_for_calvary: Either the gala was cancelled/moved or re-booked; confirm with Calvary. It explains most of the FY25 contribution drop.

finding: Filed institutional grants to Calvary have stayed near $1M a year from 26-29 funders, and one funder (GWCF incl. the Health Equity Fund) is 27% of five-year filed grants; the top five are 63%.
evidence_summary: TY2020-24 filed grants $4.43M from 50 funders; institutional $3.34M, DAF $1.09M; HHI 1168.
implication_for_calvary: Private revenue is both flat and concentrated: broadening the institutional base is as important as growing it.

finding: The FY22 revenue spike ($8.87M) was a one-time $3.68M SLFRF award for the New Foundations building, not operating growth.
evidence_summary: FY22 audit government revenue $5.69M; Treasury SLFRF subaward $3,680,675 (2022-03-08); property and equipment $2.74M -> $6.33M; net assets +$4.32M.
implication_for_calvary: Exclude FY22 from growth baselines; the building is an asset, not recurring revenue.

finding: DWC grew from $6.31M (FY2014) to $34.40M (FY2024) while its government share rose from 24% to 57%; its federal money is 99% pass-through (HUD CoC, ESG, VOCA), the same channels Calvary uses.
implication_for_calvary: The CEO's model comparator scaled with government rather than away from it, carrying 2-3 months of cash; the transferable parts are the housing pipeline (PSH development), the women's health clinic partnership and the MADE social enterprise, not the mix.

finding: The SheWorks parent (CBWC Empowerment Institute, founded 2022) is 70% government at $1.84M revenue, down from 88% in its first year, with private contributions rising from $169K to $558K; SheWorks itself launched in late 2025 with labor-federation and health-plan partners, so its funding will only appear in TY2025+ filings.
evidence_summary: m10_01; notes_for_analysis §8
implication_for_calvary: SheWorks is a program design to borrow (stipends, childcare, ride credits, employer and health-plan partners), not a funding model to copy; Calvary's Step Up DC is the natural host.

finding: Calvary's recurring government awards rose from $0.9M (2019) to about $4.1M (2024) across three channels: OVSJG, HUD CoC via TCP, and DHS via TCP.
evidence_summary: OVSJG recurring $0.37M FY20 -> $1.05M FY26; CoC $0.24M (2019 awards) -> $1.77M (FY2025 awards); DHS/TCP $1.42M in FY2024.
implication_for_calvary: Three channels, two pass-through intermediaries (TCP for both CoC and DHS) and one direct grantor: concentration sits in TCP more than in any single program.

finding: In FY24-FY25 Calvary recognized only about 73%-67% of its known award ceilings as revenue.
evidence_summary: FY24 ceilings $3.60M vs recognized $2.62M; FY25 $4.29M vs $2.89M. Line 1e matched audits in FY22-23, so the 990 figure is credible.
implication_for_calvary: Either awards are drawn below ceiling (utilization, timing, cost-reimbursement limits) or the DHS carry-forward assumption overstates FY25; both are worth asking Calvary, because undrawn awards are the cheapest revenue to recover.

finding: DC's budgets behind Calvary's local streams stayed flat to rising through FY2027, but the Mayor proposed cuts to victim services and DV lines in both FY2026 and FY2027 and the Council restored them.
evidence_summary: OVSJG Victim Services grants approved $45.5M FY24, $55.9M FY25, $55.4M FY26, $55.3M FY27; Mayor's FY26 proposal $50.1M; DHS continuum $170M FY24 -> $206M FY26; PSH ~$145-166M.
implication_for_calvary: The local risk is annual political, not structural: a Council-restoration dependency, with actual spending running 9-14% under approved.

finding: Calvary receives about 5% of DC's CoC awards and about 1% of OVSJG's awards.
evidence_summary: CoC share 5.3% (FY2025, $1.77M of $33.5M); OVSJG share 1.1% (FY2026, $1.05M of $96.7M).
implication_for_calvary: Calvary is a price-taker in both pools; growth comes from winning projects in competitions it does not control, not from pool growth.

finding: A non-renewed DHS/TCP contract would remove about $0.96M (19% of revenue); the combined worst case removes $1.31M and leaves roughly 1.7 months of cash after one year even with 50% cost avoidance.
evidence_summary: Baseline FY25: revenue $4.97M, expenses $5.58M, cash $2.06M, deficit $-0.61M. OVSJG -10% costs $0.07M; CoC -15% $0.18M.
implication_for_calvary: The DHS/TCP contract is the single largest exposure and the least documented; the OVSJG cuts that make headlines are survivable, a TCP contract loss is not without new money or cuts.

finding: Sisters Rise (24 EHV-paired PSH beds in the HIC; DHS contract capacity 25; $593K in FY2024) disappeared from the 2025 Housing Inventory Count.
evidence_summary: supp_hic_projects: 'CWS - Sisters Rise - PSH' 24 beds in 2024, absent in 2025; EHV is a sunsetting federal voucher program.
implication_for_calvary: Confirm with Calvary whether the EHV program ended in FY25; if so, part of the FY25 revenue drop is already this.

finding: Calvary's government share (53%, FY2022-24 mean) ranks 11 of 19 DC-area organizations: below every DC DV provider (DASH 70%, My Sister's Place 83%, DC SAFE 89%) and above the philanthropy-led models (Christ House, Thrive DC, Miriam's Kitchen).
evidence_summary: m3_00_benchmark_table: DC SAFE 89%, My Sister's Place 83%, Everyone Home DC 76%, N Street Village 42%, Samaritan Inns 44%, Miriam's Kitchen ~1%.
implication_for_calvary: Calvary is 'mixed', not an outlier; the exposure problem is concentration in three streams plus a thin private base, not an unusual share.

finding: Against the broader sector Calvary is typical: its government share is near the median of DC human-services organizations and of national women's/DV organizations.
evidence_summary: DC sector, FY2023: median 37%, Calvary 51% at the 57% percentile (n=163); Size-matched national, FY2022: median 56%, Calvary 61% at the 57% percentile (n=334); National women's/DV orgs, FY2022: median 65%, Calvary 61% at the 46% percentile (n=542)
implication_for_calvary: The board should not read the government share itself as a crisis; the fragility is in the streams and the cash.

finding: Calvary's real revenue growth FY19-FY24 (+13.8%/yr) trails only My Sister's Place, DWC and DC SAFE; Miriam's Kitchen grew 12% a year with almost no government money.
evidence_summary: m3_03_real_growth
implication_for_calvary: Growth has been possible on both models; the choice is about durability and cash, not growth.

finding: Calvary's liquidity (5.2 months FY2024, 4.4 in FY2025) is mid-pack; government-anchored DV providers run on about one month of cash or less, while Doorways, N Street Village and Everyone Home DC hold 8-12 months.
evidence_summary: m3_04_months_of_cash
implication_for_calvary: Peers with Calvary's mix hold more cash; a 6-month reserve target is in line with the better-capitalized mixed peers.

finding: Calvary already works institutional funders harder than most peers: 42 institutional funders TY2020-24 and filed institutional grants equal to 12% of revenue, versus 8% at House of Ruth DC, 6% at N Street Village and 11% at Miriam's Kitchen; only Samaritan Inns (27%) is far ahead.
evidence_summary: m3_06_institutional_base
implication_for_calvary: More of the same (more foundation applications) has limited headroom; the upside is larger multi-year grants from the funders in the gap list (M5), DAF/individual giving where N Street Village and Miriam's Kitchen lead, and earned revenue as at Samaritan Inns.

finding: Three replicable paths among peers: Samaritan Inns replaced government (72% -> 11%) with program and private revenue while holding revenue; N Street Village grew on private money at a stable ~40% share; DWC and House of Ruth MD scaled with government rising above 55%.
evidence_summary: m3_08_case_studies_mix; m3_05_gov_share_trajectories
implication_for_calvary: Calvary's realistic path is N Street Village's (grow private alongside government) with elements of Samaritan Inns' earned revenue; DWC shows that scaling with government needs a much larger balance sheet.

finding: DMV funders put about $132.10M a year into DC-sector organizations TY2020-24 ($660.49M total): 58% through DAF sponsors and 42% from 555 institutional funders.
evidence_summary: m4_01, m4_02: by year and funder type
implication_for_calvary: The pool is large relative to Calvary's $1M/yr of filed grants; the constraint is access, not supply.

finding: The institutional pool is concentrated: the top 10 funders give 55% of institutional dollars to the DC sector, and 6 of the top 25 already fund Calvary.
implication_for_calvary: Calvary's institutional coverage of the majors is already broad; the next wins are the large non-funders on the list (Clark, Weinberg, Casey, Wal-Mart, Morningstar) and deeper grants from current majors.

finding: The typical institutional grant to a DC-sector organization is small (median $10K); six-figure grants are the top decile and come from community and private foundations.
implication_for_calvary: Moving the needle by $0.5M needs a handful of six-figure, multi-year relationships, not dozens of new $10K grants.

finding: Fidelity Charitable moved $179.22M into DC-sector organizations in five years, more than any foundation; DAF money is a donor-cultivation channel, not a grant pipeline.
implication_for_calvary: Calvary's DAF receipts ($1.1M over five years, 25% of filed grants) track individual major donors; growth there is a major-gifts strategy.

finding: Most institutional money to the DC sector is general operating or untagged; grants whose purpose names housing, DV or women are a minority, and the biggest mission-tagged funders are Maryland and Virginia foundations that give little in DC.
implication_for_calvary: Mission language alone will not find the money; the funders to target are the DC general-support givers who already fund peers.

finding: 23 institutional funders give to three or more of Calvary's 18 peers and have no filed grant to Calvary; 75 give to two or more.
evidence_summary: m5_01: Venable Foundation (10 peers), T. Rowe Price Program (8), Gifts for the Homeless (8), Capital Area Food Bank (7), America's Charities (7), Clark Charitable (5 peers, $7.8M), Schattner, Bunting, Bechtel, Cohen, Bernstein, Washington Home.
implication_for_calvary: These are the warmest cold prospects: they fund Calvary's model already. Several (Venable, America's Charities) are in the CRM, so the filing gap is partly lag.

finding: 12 former institutional funders filed itemized grant lists since TY2023 with nothing for Calvary; they once gave $0.26M in total.
evidence_summary: m5_02; World Bank Community Connections Fund, Many Hands Inc, Jane Bancroft Robinson Foundation Inc, Robert M Fisher Memorial Foundation Inc, The Junior League Of The City Of Washington Inc, Levatus Charitable Trust
implication_for_calvary: Re-engagement is cheaper than acquisition; check the CRM for gifts routed through DAFs or corporate channels first.

finding: 15 of Calvary's current institutional funders have written larger single grants to a core peer than to Calvary.
evidence_summary: m5_03: largest grant to Calvary vs largest grant to a peer, TY2020-24
implication_for_calvary: An upgrade ask to known funders is the fastest institutional money; pair it with the multi-year framing.

finding: Only 44% of the CRM's $10.6M in 2023-26 institutional giving is verifiable in funders' own filings; corporate givers with no public filing (MGAC, IMF, Latham, Frontier Co-op) are $2.6M and 'see attached' filers (Philip L. Graham, Clark-Winchcole, Kay, Herb Block) $1.3M.
evidence_summary: m5_06 (supp_crm_cash_verification)
implication_for_calvary: Corporate relationships are a larger share of Calvary's private money than the filings show; the pipeline must treat them as a separate, relationship-led track.

finding: The funder web around Calvary and its peers has 330 funders; the most connected institutional funders (GWCF 18 of 19 organizations, Cafritz 14, Venable 10, Abell 9) already fund Calvary except Venable, and the DAF sponsors (Fidelity, Benevity, Schwab) connect almost everyone.
evidence_summary: m6_01_central_funders
implication_for_calvary: Calvary is already inside the core of the DC human-services funder web; the next funders are one step away through peers it shares funders with.

finding: Calvary shares the most institutional funders with Miriam's Kitchen (17), DASH (14) and House of Ruth DC (14); House of Ruth DC and House of Ruth MD have the longest lists of institutional funders Calvary lacks.
evidence_summary: m6_02_cofunding_overlap
implication_for_calvary: Those peers' funder lists are the best-evidenced prospect lists: a funder that gives to three organizations with Calvary's profile is likely to consider a fourth.

finding: Board interlocks are a thin channel: Calvary has 8 shared-board links in filings, 1 at high confidence (none with a funder); 7 medium-confidence links include Washington Area Women's Foundation, United Way NCA, United Way of Central Maryland and Miriam's Kitchen.
evidence_summary: m6_04_board_interlocks; candidate_interlocks has no Calvary rows
implication_for_calvary: Relationship paths in the leadership materials rest on shared funders, not boards; the medium-confidence links go to the consulting team as leads to confirm.

finding: The scored pipeline has 182 rows: 11 Tier 1 (pursue now), 40 Tier 2, 131 Tier 3. Tier 1 institutional targets (7): William S Abell Foundation, Greater Washington Community Foundation, Clark Charitable Foundation, Morris And Gwendolyn Cafritz Foundation, John Edward Fowler Memorial Foundation, Robert I Schattner Foundation, Americas Charities.
evidence_summary: recommendations/funder_pipeline.csv
implication_for_calvary: Weights are editable in config/scoring_weights.yaml; the ranking is a starting point for the development team's judgment, not a verdict on any funder.

finding: The adjacent areas Calvary already touches (DV, behavioral health, workforce, education) carry about $149.22M a year of DMV institutional grants whose purpose names them; physical health is the largest pool one step further ($84.15M/yr, 206 funders at $100K+).
evidence_summary: m8_01_expansion_scan
implication_for_calvary: Formalizing what Calvary already does (workforce, behavioral health, DV designation) opens funders without changing the mission; health and aging need a partner or credential.

finding: The Grants.gov feed yields only 36 relevant federal notices across all areas after filtering; the federal path for Calvary runs through DC intermediaries (TCP, OVSJG, DHS), not direct competition.
evidence_summary: m8_02_federal_opportunities
implication_for_calvary: Direct federal grants are a Tier 3 option; HUD CoC via TCP and HUD CPF earmarks are the realistic federal channels.

finding: Calvary's service area carries the city's deepest need: Ward 8 poverty 31% and Ward 7 23% against 15% for DC; female poverty 32% in Ward 8; a third of renters in both wards pay over half their income in rent.
evidence_summary: m9_01_ward_indicators
implication_for_calvary: The case statement for place-based funders (Bainum, Cafritz, GWCF, Clark) is strong and quantified.

finding: DC's homeless count fell from 8,350 (2016) to 5,138 (2025) while Calvary's inventory grew to 124 beds and 7% of DC's transitional-housing beds.
evidence_summary: m9_02_dc_pit; m9_03_calvary_hic_share
implication_for_calvary: Calvary has become a system-level provider for single women; that position is the argument for durable public contracts and for PSH expansion.
